text: A digital twin framework consists of a physical system; a high-fidelity model (such as CFD) referred to as a digital shadow; an inverse modeling framework to take physical system measurements and learn parameters such as HTC, friction factors, etc; and a reduced-order model (ROM) that lives between the high-fidelity model and the experiment as a fast prediction and system surrogate. This project is primarily concerned with ROMs and order reduction methods as a way to leverage high-fidelity physics insight to better elucidate live experimental results and assist with predictive operations.

A state is a weighted representation of a heater region, leg, cooler region, or possible thermal bridge. My physical network has separate axial fluid, pipe and insulation nodes, plus explicit heater, ambient, and jacket paths where applicable. A regional state may predict relaxation and settling well, but comparing it with a wall thermocouple is a model-adequacy test, not proof it independently predicts wall and fluid temperatures.”

text: 2:00–3:15 — Explain the identifiability issue simply. “In a passive cooldown, the measured speed is governed mainly by conductance divided by capacity. Doubling both gives the same temperature curve: (C\dot\theta=-A\theta) and ((2C)\dot\theta=-(2A)\theta). More passive repeats can tighten a time constant, but cannot determine both absolute scales from that curve alone. Nick fixes inventories and nominal resistances where practical, which can supply an external scale if those priors are trusted; the passive data alone do not establish it. A measured nonzero power history or an accepted steady energy balance supplies an absolute anchor. Even then, individual regional parameters need sensitivity and holdout evidence.”

In my physical-model sequence, steady measured-power cases first constrain grouped conductances; dynamic tests then address capacities.
